Hebrew
HEE-broo
noun / adjective
Hebrew Ivri (עברי), probably derived from Eber (עבר), the ancestor of Abraham mentioned in Genesis 10:24–25, or from the root ’ābar (עבר), “to cross over” — denoting one who crossed the River Euphrates or some other boundary. Abram is the first person in Scripture called “the Hebrew” (Gen 14:13), establishing the term as a patrilineal identity marker. The word passed through Greek Hebraios (Ἑβραῖος) and Latin Hebraeus into English “Hebrew,” serving as both the name of the people and the name of their sacred language.

Biblical Definition

Scripture first applies “Hebrew” to Abram after the rescue of Lot: “And there came one that had escaped, and told Abram the Hebrew; for he dwelt in the plain of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol, and brother of Aner: and these were confederate with Abram.” (Gen 14:13) — a designation that distinguishes him from the Canaanite peoples and grounds his identity in covenant lineage. The term recurs at key moments of national identity: the midwives of Egypt (Exod 1:16), the infant Moses floating in the Nile (Exod 2:6), and Joseph named to Potiphar's household (Gen 39:14) are all identified as Hebrews, marking ethnic and covenantal solidarity in the face of pagan opposition.

Paul claimed the term as a badge of confessional honor: “a Hebrew of Hebrews” (Phil 3:5) — not merely of Hebrew descent but of undiluted Hebrew-speaking lineage, contrasted with the Hellenistic Jews who had adopted Greek language and culture. Acts 6:1 records the early church's own use of the distinction: native Hebrews and Hellenistic Jews were the two streams of the Jerusalem congregation, and the friction between them prompted the appointment of the seven deacons.

The Hebrew language is the tongue in which God gave the Torah, the Psalms, and the Prophets — the Masoretic Text of the Old Testament, the providentially preserved Hebrew Scriptures. Reformed confessionalism (1689 LBCF 1.8) holds the Hebrew Old Testament as the authentic text by which all translations are to be tested. The language itself carries the impress of divine revelation: its verbal structures (perfect and imperfect, qal and niphal) shape the grammar of promise and fulfillment, command and consequence, that runs through all of biblical theology.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines Hebrew as pertaining to the Hebrews, the descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; also, the language of that people, the original tongue of the Old Testament Scriptures, and of all ancient biblical revelation.

HEBREW, n. [from Heber, the progenitor, or from the root meaning to pass over.] A descendant of Shem through Eber and Abraham; the name given to Abraham and his posterity, who later received the name Israelites from Jacob's divine title, and Jews from the tribe of Judah during and after the Babylonian captivity.

HEBREW, n. The language of the ancient Hebrews; a Semitic language written right-to-left in a consonantal script subsequently supplemented with Masoretic vowel pointing; the primary language of the Old Testament canon, with Aramaic sections in Ezra, Daniel, and Jeremiah.

The Hebrew Scriptures — the thirty-nine books of the Old Testament in the original language — are the providentially preserved textual foundation of all Christian theology; Reformed confessionalism holds the Masoretic Hebrew text as authentic and authoritative, the measure against which all translations and interpretations must be tested.

Key Scripture

Gen 14:13 — "And there came one that had escaped, and told Abram the Hebrew; for he dwelt in the plain of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol, and brother of Aner: and these were confederate with Abram."

Phil 3:5 — "Circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, an Hebrew of the Hebrews; as touching the law, a Pharisee;"

Acts 6:1 — "And in those days, when the number of the disciples was multiplied, there arose a murmuring of the Grecians against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily ministration."

John 5:2 — "Now there is at Jerusalem by the sheep market a pool, which is called in the Hebrew tongue Bethesda, having five porches."

Modern Corruption

Academic biblical studies frequently treat “Hebrew” as a merely ethnic or linguistic category evacuated of covenantal significance; modern supersessionism from the opposite direction dissolves the Hebrew identity of the OT people into a purely typological function, flattening the genuine continuity between Israel and the church.

expand to see more

Historical-critical scholarship uses “Hebrew” primarily as a linguistic and archaeological category — the “Hebrew Bible” in place of “Old Testament,” the “ancient Hebrew people” studied via Ancient Near Eastern comparison rather than canonical narrative. This approach strips the covenantal weight from the category: Abram is “the Hebrew” not merely as an ethnic marker but as the bearer of the divine promise (Gen 12:1–3), the friend of God (James 2:23), the father of the faithful (Rom 4:16). To read the Hebrew identity through anthropological categories rather than covenantal ones is to misread the text at its foundation.

A second corruption comes from certain supersessionist theologies that treat Hebrew identity as purely preparatory, with no ongoing significance for the church's self-understanding or its reading of Scripture. Reformed covenant theology insists otherwise: the church is grafted into the covenant made with Abraham (Rom 11:17–18); the Hebrew Scriptures are the church's canon, not a superseded document; the Psalms are to be sung in Christian worship as the inheritance of the covenant people. Paul's pride in being “a Hebrew of Hebrews” (Phil 3:5) does not evacuate the category — he counts it loss for Christ's sake (Phil 3:7), but loss presupposes genuine value.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew identity is traced through Eber and Abraham, the covenant lineage from which the Scriptures, the Law, the Prophets, and the Savior all emerged; the Hebrew language is the vessel in which God cast the grammar of His self-revelation.

expand to see more

Hebrew Ivri (עברי) — “one from across” or “descendant of Eber”; first applied to Abraham in Gen 14:13, establishing a distinction between the covenant bearer and the surrounding Canaanite peoples; the term carried ethnic, linguistic, and religious freight throughout the OT era

Eber (עבר) — the great-grandson of Shem (Gen 10:21–24), ancestor of the Hebrews and the Eberite genealogical line through Peleg and Reu to Abraham; the name possibly derives from ’ābar (“to cross over”), suggesting a people defined by boundary-crossing under covenant call

The Masoretic Text — the vowel-pointed Hebrew manuscript tradition standardized by the Masoretes (600–1000 AD) from earlier textual families; the textus receptus of the Old Testament, preserved by Jewish scribes with extraordinary care and accepted by the Reformation as the authentic OT canon

Hebrew as the language of prophecy — the prophetic corpus of Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and the Twelve was given in Hebrew, making that language the medium of eschatological promise; the NT authors, citing the LXX or translating directly from the Hebrew, demonstrate that the Hebrew text is the controlling authority behind every apostolic argument

Paul as “Hebrew of Hebrews” (Phil 3:5) — Paul's self-identification signals both linguistic purity (Aramaic-speaking heritage, not merely diaspora Greek-speaking) and confessional integrity before his Damascus Road encounter; his counting all this “rubbish” (Phil 3:8) for Christ demonstrates the surpassing worth of knowing Him, not the worthlessness of Hebrew covenant heritage

Usage

"The Epistle to the Hebrews takes its title from its primary audience — Jewish Christians tempted to revert to the Mosaic economy — and its argument turns on the Hebrew Scriptures themselves, demonstrating from Psalm 110, Jeremiah 31, and Leviticus that the old covenant was designed to be surpassed by the new covenant it anticipated."

"The Reformation insistence on ad fontes — back to the sources — included the recovery of Hebrew scholarship in the Western church; Reuchlin, Bucer, and Calvin all studied Hebrew as the necessary tool for reading the Old Testament on its own terms rather than through the Vulgate's Latin mediation."

"The Westminster Confession (1.8) specifies the Hebrew Old Testament as one of two authenticating texts for all versions: “The Old Testament in Hebrew (which was the native language of the people of God of old)... being immediately inspired by God, and by His singular care and providence kept pure in all ages, [is] therefore authentical.”"
